title: Breakfast on the beach (John 21:1–19)
hookLine: by a charcoal fire, Jesus asks Peter three times: do you love me?
last: DOUBT IS ALLOWED IN THE ROOM.

cards: Some things between friends never get mentioned. They just sit there. By the sea of Tiberias, in Galilee, some days after the empty tomb, Peter says he's going fishing, and six of the others go with him.
All night, nothing. At dawn a figure on the beach calls: throw the net on the right side of the boat. It fills so heavily they can't haul it in.
One of them says, it is the Lord, and Peter pulls on his coat and jumps into the water. On the shore a fire is already burning, with fish on it, and bread: come and have breakfast.
But something still sits between Peter and Jesus, and the fire is the kind Peter has seen before.

teach.b: John uses one Greek word for a charcoal fire at two moments.

The first is the night of the arrest, in the high priest's courtyard, where Peter warms his hands and says three times that he doesn't know Jesus. The second is this beach: same fire, same smell of smoke.
After they eat, Jesus asks, in the King James Bible: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?" Yes, Lord, you know I love you. Feed my lambs.
He asks again. And a third time.

Readers can hardly miss the match with three denials. John says Peter was grieved at the third, and he answers like someone with nothing left to prove: "Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee."
And Jesus says, "Feed my sheep." Nobody brings up the courtyard. No lecture, no probation.
Each yes is answered with a job: look after the people I love.
John's Greek uses two verbs for love here, agapao and phileo, and readers argue about whether it matters. Some hear a shift in the kind of love; others think John just varies his words, as elsewhere.

Churches hear the charge differently: Catholics and Orthodox Christians hear feed my sheep as Peter given a shepherd's work in the church, and many Protestants hear it above all as a picture of what grace does for anyone who has failed.
What they share is the shape: three denials, three loves, and then a future.

how: Many Christians read John 21 as the story of Peter's restoration after his denials, and preachers often use it to speak about forgiveness and second chances. Catholics and Orthodox Christians also read 'feed my sheep' as part of Peter's commission to lead.

o: the altar fire kept burning in the temple
a signal fire to guide the fishing boats home
a fire like the one where Peter denied Jesus

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: where Peter denied, and where he's restored

s: Jesus reminds Peter of his three denials
he never mentions them. he asks three times, do you love me, and answers each yes with a job.
John uses the same word for a charcoal fire at the denial and on this beach
the same kind of fire twice: once where Peter denied him, once where he's restored.
everyone agrees the two Greek words for love change the meaning
readers disagree. some hear a shift; others think John simply varies his words.

games.q: you're Peter. you denied him three times. now he's cooked you breakfast, and he asks: do you love me? what do you say?
o: nothing. you've lost the right to answer.
yes, Lord, you know that I love you.
games.why: Peter says yes, three times, the last time grieved: "Lord, thou knowest all things." each yes is met with a job: feed my sheep.

practice: Picture someone who let you down, nothing huge, at breakfast with you, a fire going, the thing not yet mentioned. Without pretending it didn't happen, picture handing them something to do again, a little trust back.
If you pray, bring their name to God; if not, hold the picture and notice how it sits in you.

wordCard.voice: Charcoal fire. The kind of fire where Peter denied knowing Jesus three times, burning again on the beach where Jesus asks him three questions.

orig.note: Greek: a charcoal fire. John uses it at the night of the denial and again on this beach.

carryVoice: Your line: three denials, three loves. Tomorrow, he's lifted out of sight. Day seventy-three, done.
